w:r.w:t: The University of Eastminster currently relies on a static HTML page to present information about its graduates to the wider student community. While functional at a basic level, this approach fails to reflect the dynamic nature of modern alumni networks or the professional achievements that graduates accumulate over time. Phantasmagoria Ltd, a London-based educational technology company, has been contracted to replace this system with a fully interactive, API-driven platform that transforms how students discover and connect with alumni.

The new platform reframes alumni not merely as past students, but as active influencers within a professional marketplace. Graduates with strong LinkedIn profiles, industry certifications, and accredited licences can leverage their credentials on the platform, supported by sponsorship from professional course providers and certification bodies. These sponsors fund alumni bids for daily featured exposure, creating a self-sustaining economy of professional inspiration for current students.

From a technical standpoint, the platform is built as a RESTful web API using Node.js and Express.js, making it client-agnostic by design. As covered in the Week 7 lecture on REST, separating the data producer from the consumer allows the same backend to serve multiple front-end surfaces simultaneously in this case, a browser-based alumni dashboard, an administrative panel, and an external augmented reality client provided by the university.
The existing static alumni page presents several fundamental limitations that reduce its effectiveness as an engagement tool:
Alumni information is manually maintained and quickly becomes outdated, with no mechanism for graduates to update their own records.
Students have no way to filter, explore, or interact with alumni profiles, resulting in low engagement with the page.
There is no recognition or incentive system to encourage alumni to keep their profiles current or participate in university initiatives.
The system is entirely disconnected from modern professional networks such as LinkedIn, making it impossible to reflect real-world career progression.
No developer API exists, meaning the data cannot be consumed by third-party clients such as the university's planned augmented reality application.
There is no administrative layer to manage access, monitor usage, or generate usage statistics for reporting purposes.

The primary objective of this project is to design, implement, and document a secure, production-grade RESTful API that serves as the backbone of the Alumni Influencer Platform. The system must be fully client-agnostic that is, it must expose well-documented endpoints that any authorised consumer can interact with, regardless of the technology stack used on the client side.
The specific objectives of the API are as follows:

Registration and Authentication: Provide a secure self-registration flow restricted to verified university domain email addresses, including email verification, session-based login for browser clients, and JWT-based authentication for API consumers.

Profile Management: Allow alumni to build and maintain comprehensive professional profiles covering academic qualifications, industry certifications, professional licences, short courses, and full employment history, including support for profile image upload.

Blind Bidding System: Implement a fair daily bidding mechanism in which alumni compete for the Alumni of the Day featured slot using funds received from their sponsors, without visibility of competing bids.
Developer API and Token Management: Expose a public-facing API endpoint for the AR client, protected by revocable bearer tokens, with full usage logging and administrative oversight.

Automated Winner Selection: Run a scheduled midnight process that selects the highest bidder for the following day, updates the featured profile, and dispatches email notifications to all participants.

Security: Apply a comprehensive, layered security posture covering transport security, request-level validation, CSRF protection, rate limiting, bcrypt password hashing, and cryptographically secure token generation.
Documentation: Generate and serve a complete interactive Swagger/OpenAPI 3.0 specification at /api-docs, enabling third-party developers to explore and test all endpoints without reading source code.

This submission covers the full backend implementation of the Alumni Influencer Platform, including the database schema, all API routes and controllers, the security middleware stack, the bidding scheduler service, the email notification service, and the Swagger documentation layer. A lightweight frontend is included solely to demonstrate the API's functionality during the viva; it is not a deliverable in its own right.

The augmented reality client itself is outside the scope of this coursework. The API has been built to remain completely agnostic of any particular client implementation the GET /api/public/featured endpoint returns a full JSON representation of the featured alumni profile that any client can consume without modification. Similarly, the administrative API key management system allows future client applications to be onboarded and revoked independently without changes to the server code.

Horizontal scalability is addressed at the architecture level. The API is stateless by virtue of its JWT-based authentication, meaning multiple server instances can run in parallel without shared session storage. Two specific configuration requirements are documented for a production load-balanced deployment: the trust proxy setting required for correct rate limiting behind Nginx, and the restriction of the bid scheduler to a designated Primary node to prevent race conditions and duplicate winner selection.

This section presents a high-level view of the Alumni Influencer Platform, describing how the system is decomposed into layers, how those layers interact, and how the overall design meets the scalability and security requirements established in Chapter 1.

The Alumni Influencer Platform is structured as a four-layer server-side application. Each layer has a clearly defined responsibility and communicates with adjacent layers through well-defined interfaces. This separation of concerns, introduced in the Week 2 lecture on MVC architecture, ensures that changes to one layer do not propagate uncontrolled side effects to others, and that the system can be extended or scaled at any individual layer independently.

Two distinct client surfaces are supported. The Alumni Portal is a browser-based interface through which registered alumni manage their profiles, monitor their bid status, and review their bidding history. The Developer Hub provides administrative access to API token management and usage statistics. Both surfaces communicate with the backend exclusively through HTTP requests no business logic is embedded in the client code. This design directly supports the REST principle covered in the Week 7 lecture, in which the consumer of data is fully decoupled from its producer.

All inbound requests pass through a security middleware stack before reaching any application logic. Helmet.js sets fourteen HTTP security headers automatically on every response. CORS middleware restricts cross-origin access to whitelisted origins defined in the environment configuration. A custom synchroniser-token CSRF implementation, based on the token approach described in the Week 10 lecture, protects all state-changing endpoints against cross-site request forgery. express-rate-limit applies per-IP request throttling 20 requests per 15-minute window on authentication routes and 100 on general routes mitigating brute-force and denial-of-service attempts. express-validator sanitises and type-checks all incoming request bodies before a single line of controller code executes.

The application layer is implemented in Node.js with Express.js and follows the MVC-inspired structure described in Chapter 3. Five controller modules handle the five functional domains of the system: authentication, profile management, bidding, administration, and public access. Two services operate alongside the controllers: the emailService dispatches transactional email using Nodemailer over Gmail SMTP, and the bidScheduler runs a node-cron task at midnight each day to resolve the winning bid, update the featured profile, and notify all participants. In a horizontally scaled deployment, the scheduler is restricted to the Primary instance via a NODE_ROLE environment check to prevent concurrent execution across multiple nodes.

All persistent data is stored in a MySQL relational database accessed through a mysql2 connection pool. The schema is normalised to Third Normal Form, with multi-valued profile attributes such as degrees, certifications, licences, courses, and employment history each held in dedicated child tables. Profile images uploaded by alumni are stored on the local filesystem in the /uploads directory and served as static files by Express. In a production deployment, this would be replaced by object storage such as AWS S3.

The system is intentionally designed for horizontal scalability. Because all session state is encoded in signed JWT tokens rather than stored server-side, any number of Node.js instances can process requests simultaneously without requiring a shared session store. The sole stateful component, the bid scheduler, is designed to run on exactly one designated node, isolating the risk of race conditions to a single, controllable point in the architecture.

This section outlines the architectural approach adopted for the Alumni Influencers Platform, the rationale for using an MVC-based structure, and the internal organisation of the backend. The purpose of this section is to demonstrate how the application is structured to achieve maintainability, modularity, and secure request processing.

The system follows a client-server architecture where the frontend handles user interaction and the backend exposes RESTful endpoints for processing requests, enforcing security, and interacting with the database. As described in the Week 1 lecture on web applications, clients make requests over HTTP and servers fulfil those requests and respond. This separation improves maintainability, scalability, and security by keeping all business logic on the server side.

The platform is implemented as a layered monolithic application, organised into routing, middleware, controllers, services, and data layers. This structure improves code organisation and directly supports the MVC pattern covered in Week 2, where models, views, and controllers occupy distinct, well-defined roles.
The backend adopts an MVC-inspired architectural structure to maintain a clear separation of concerns:

: The model layer is represented by the MySQL relational database and the direct SQL database access logic. It is responsible for storing and retrieving all application data including user accounts, alumni profiles, bids, API keys, and usage logs.

In this project, the view layer is represented by the client-side interface. It provides the pages and interactive components through which alumni and developers access the system. Since the frontend communicates with the backend through HTTP requests, it remains fully decoupled from business logic.

The controller layer acts as the bridge between incoming requests and the underlying data and service logic. Controllers validate inputs, invoke business rules, coordinate database operations, and generate appropriate HTTP responses.

The MVC approach was chosen because it improves maintainability and makes the codebase easier to scale. New features can be introduced with minimal impact on unrelated parts of the system. For example, a mobile application could reuse the same backend controllers and models without any redesign of the core logic.
Every HTTP request follows the same deterministic pipeline. The diagram below shows each stage from client request to JSON response, with the associated module at each layer.

The system uses a modular routing structure where requests are grouped based on functionality: authentication, profile management, bidding, developer API, and public endpoints. This improves maintainability and keeps the application organised, as recommended by the Express.js framework taught in the Week 8 lecture.

Each request follows a middleware flow before reaching the business logic. As described in the Week 8 lecture, middleware functions have access to the request object, response object, and the next function in the cycle. This middleware layer handles authentication, validation, and security checks before passing control to the appropriate controller.

The authentication layer, built using JWT tokens and sessions as covered in the Week 10 lecture, ensures that protected routes can only be accessed by authorised users. JWT was chosen because, unlike session-based authentication, it does not require server-side storage and is therefore better suited to stateless, multi-client API architectures.

The system uses a MySQL relational database to ensure structured data storage, integrity, and efficient querying. A relational database was selected because the system contains clearly defined relationships between users, profiles, bids, and API access records.

The database follows Third Normal Form (3NF) to reduce redundancy and maintain data consistency. Relationships are established using primary and foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE to ensure referential integrity across the system. Multi-valued attributes such as degrees, certifications, licences, courses, and employment history occupy dedicated child tables, eliminating repeating groups. The main entities in the database include:
Users credentials, verification tokens, and role assignment
Profiles professional alumni data, LinkedIn URL, and featured status
Bids blind bidding records with UNIQUE(user_id, slot_date) constraint
API Keys SHA-256 hashed bearer tokens with revocation support
Usage Logs full audit trail of all API key activity by endpoint and timestamp

The system exposes RESTful API endpoints to handle authentication, profile management, bidding functionality, and developer API access. As established in the Week 7 REST lecture, these endpoints follow uniform interface principles and use standard HTTP methods to convey intent: GET for retrieval, POST for creation, PUT/PATCH for updates, and DELETE for removal. All endpoints return JSON representations with appropriate HTTP status codes.
Register new alumni with university email; sends verification link
Validates single-use token from email and marks account as verified
bcrypt compare; returns JWT; sets session role for browser clients
Sends password reset email with 1-hour time-limited token
Validates reset token; updates password hash; invalidates token
Fetch full profile for authenticated alumnus
Update biography, LinkedIn URL, and personal details
Upload profile photo via multer; stored to /uploads directory
Add, edit, delete degree entries (same pattern for certs, licences, employment)
Place a blind bid for the next day slot; enforces monthly limit check
Increase an existing active bid; new amount must exceed current amount
Cancel an active bid for today
Returns WINNING or LOSING; highest bid amount is never disclosed
Full personal bid history with outcomes
Generate new API bearer token (SHA-256 hash stored, raw returned once)
List all tokens with last_used_at and revocation status
Revoke an API key immediately by setting is_revoked to TRUE
Full audit log of all API key usage by endpoint and timestamp
Returns today's featured alumni profile for the AR client (Bearer API key)

The bidding system is the core business differentiator. Fairness is maintained by ensuring no bidder can see the current highest bid, they only receive a binary WINNING / LOSING status based on whether their bid is currently the highest for the upcoming date.

• Proxy Configuration: To support production deployments behind Nginx or other reverse proxies, the system implements ‘app.set('trust proxy', 1)’ in app.js. This ensures that security middleware like express-rate-limit correctly identifies the remote client’s IP address from the X-Forwarded-For header, preventing the system from misidentifying the load balancer as the sole client and blocking all traffic.

• Scalability Status: The API is designed for horizontal scalability through its stateless JWT implementation. By using signed tokens for authentication rather than server-side session persistence for API requests, the backend can be cloned across multiple server instances without requiring complex session synchronization or "sticky sessions," allowing for seamless elastic scaling.

• Race Condition Risk: The startScheduler() function currently triggers the midnight bid processing logic on every server boot. In a horizontally scaled environment, this would cause multiple instances to attempt to select winners simultaneously. To mitigate this risk, scheduler execution is restricted to a single "Primary" node via an environment check (IS_PRIMARY_NODE), ensuring bid processing and winner emails are handled exactly once.

This project successfully implements a secure and scalable Alumni Influencers Platform API. The system supports alumni registration, profile management, blind bidding, developer API access, and automated winner selection via a nightly cron job.

The architecture applies principles taught throughout the 6COSC022W module: the client-server model from Week 1, the MVC separation of concerns from Week 2, the REST uniform interface principles from Week 7, the Express.js middleware architecture from Week 8, and the JWT, session, and CSRF protection techniques from Week 10. Security mechanisms including Helmet.js headers, CORS whitelisting, CSRF synchroniser tokens, bcrypt password hashing, JWT bearer authentication, SHA-256 API key hashing, parameterised SQL queries, and rate limiting are all applied in layers, providing defence-in-depth.

The MySQL database follows Third Normal Form, eliminating redundancy through dedicated child tables for all multi-valued profile attributes. The Swagger/OpenAPI 3.0 interactive documentation at /api-docs provides a complete reference for the AR client and future API consumers. The system is designed for extensibility: the stateless JWT-based API can be scaled horizontally, and the modular controller structure allows new features to be added with minimal impact on existing components.
